newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish family firms duck as wealth tax bites.
newsitem.headline: Swedish family firms duck as wealth tax bites.

text.p: Seeking to escape the sharp bite of a new wealth tax, family-controlled Swedish companies are fleeing the Stockholm bourse's main A list and sprinting for the protection of the smaller O list.

Fashion retailer Hennes & Mauritz announced on Thursday it would transfer its shares while construction group Lundbergs said it would do so a day earlier and investment company Latour decided to act last week.

A new law that took effect in late 1996 forces Swedes with wealth exceeding 900,000 crowns to pay 1.5 percent tax on 100 percent of the value of shares listed on the A list, up from 75 percent, while shares on the O list remain exempt from tax.
Other family-controlled groups could follow suit, even though the shares of some companies that have announced the move have fallen.
"I think more companies will transfer their shares," Ulf Lindgren, chief legal counsel at the Stockholm Stock Exchange, told Reuters.
"We don't have any more applications at the moment but we have got questions from company advisors indicating such moves."
This means families could be forced to sell part of their stakes to be able to pay the new tax.

"Stefan Persson (the chief executive and main owner of Hennes & Mauritz) was very close to paying 100 percent of his income in tax last year and is very close this year too," Hennes & Mauritz spokesman Jan Jacobsen said.

"A growth company like Hennes & Mauritz pays a fairly low dividend as it needs the money to expand, so the dividend does not make up for the wealth tax," he said. There is also a 30 percent tax on dividends.
H&M's capital is about 38 percent owned by Stefan Persson and his family and the family controls about 70 percent of the voting rights. Persson's father founded the company.

The recent transfers from the A list were triggered by a law adopted by parliament last week that says main shareholders -- people holding more than 25 percent of votes -- do not have to pay tax for shares listed on the A list after 1991.
Hennes & Mauritz was listed on the A list before 1991 so Stefan Persson is liable to tax.
"We waited with transferring the shares because we hoped the government would change the 1996 tax when it presented the new tax in May," Jacobsen said.
Hennes & Mauritz's plunged on the transfer announcement as some institutional investors have internal rules saying they can only invest in shares on the A list.
The share plunged to 231 crowns from 257 crowns before the announcement but closed at 234.5 crowns, down 19.5 crowns from a day earlier.
The government dismissed the transfers and said it had no intention of changing the law.
"No new legislation is on the agenda," Junior Finance Minister Thomas Ostros, responsible for tax issues, said. "It's not that important that some companies are choosing to move."
Lindgren said that although the bourse was not happy to see its main list hurt, it would not act.
The stock exchange would, however, let the companies move back to the A list if they wanted to, Lindgren said.
"We wouldn't say no if they applied," Lindgren said. "We cannot stop them if they fulfil the criteria."
-- Birgitta Forsberg, Stockholm newsroom +46-8-700 1017
